guide.title: Respiratory Emergencies
guide.lead: Breathless patients tell you how sick they are by how they talk, sit and look. Treat what you hear: wheeze, crackles or nothing at all. Then give the right amount of oxygen. A quiet asthmatic isn't better, and a COPD patient doesn't need 100%.

sections.title: Who is breathless, and why?
rows: Sudden onset, pleuritic pain, fast pulse, clear lungs
Oxygen, rapid transport, watch for collapse
Sit up, CPAP, nitrates (see Heart Failure)

groups.title: Severe
items: Speaks in words, hunched forward, agitated
Respiratory rate above 30, heart rate above 120

groups.title: Life-threatening
items: Silent chest: too little air to wheeze

steps.title: Tiring or silent chest
steps.text: Assist ventilation with a BVM; prepare for arrest.

sections.title: COPD and oxygen
items: Target 88–92% in patients at risk of CO₂ retention
Venturi mask 24–28%; drive nebulizers with air plus nasal oxygen when possible
Too much oxygen raises CO₂ by worsening ventilation-perfusion mismatch: titrate, don't withhold
Never use a paper bag for "hyperventilation": rule out PE, asthma, DKA and hypoxia first

quiz.q: An asthmatic's wheeze becomes much quieter while she gets drowsier. This means:
quiz.explanation: Too little air moves to make a wheeze. Assist ventilation.

quiz.q: Sudden breathlessness, sharp right chest pain and SpO₂ 84% after a 12-hour flight. Suspect:
quiz.explanation: Long travel is a classic risk factor.

quiz.q: A COPD patient on 15 L/min by non-rebreather becomes drowsy and her breathing slows. Most likely?
options: CO₂ retention from too much oxygen: titrate to 88–92% and support breathing
quiz.explanation: Mainly ventilation-perfusion mismatch; titrate, don't remove oxygen.

quiz.q: Target SpO₂ for most acutely breathless patients:
quiz.explanation: 88–92% for those at risk of CO₂ retention.

quiz.q: First drug for an asthma attack:
Which is a life-threatening asthma sign?
quiz.explanation: Also silent chest and falling SpO₂ despite oxygen.

quiz.q: Fever, cough with green sputum and crackles over one lung suggest:
Magnesium sulfate in severe asthma is given:
quiz.explanation: When the attack isn't responding to bronchodilators.

quiz.q: Why not use a paper bag for a hyperventilating patient?
options: It can cause hypoxia, and the cause may be serious
quiz.explanation: Rule out PE, asthma, DKA and hypoxia.

quiz.q: Which mask suits a COPD patient needing controlled oxygen?

flashcards.question: Signs of an acute asthma attack
flashcards.answer: Expiratory wheeze, prolonged expiration, accessory muscles, tripod position, short sentences, tachypnea, tachycardia.

flashcards.question: Silent chest in asthma
flashcards.answer: Too little air moving to wheeze: a late sign of impending respiratory failure. Assist ventilation.

flashcards.question: COPD: chronic vs acute
flashcards.answer: Acute exacerbation: worse breathlessness, more and purulent sputum, falling SpO₂, drowsiness (CO₂ retention).

flashcards.question: Signs of pneumonia
flashcards.answer: Fever, chills, productive cough, pleuritic pain, focal crackles, tachypnea, hypoxia.

flashcards.question: Pulmonary embolism
flashcards.answer: Sudden breathlessness, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxia, sometimes collapse. Risks: surgery, immobility, travel, cancer, pregnancy, estrogen, previous clot.

flashcards.question: Hyperventilation from anxiety
flashcards.answer: A diagnosis of exclusion: rule out PE, asthma, DKA, hypoxia. Calm reassurance; never a paper bag.

flashcards.question: CPAP in respiratory emergencies
flashcards.answer: Splints alveoli open: pulmonary edema and COPD. Not for unresponsive, apneic or hypotensive patients, or when vomiting.

flashcards.question: Oxygen targets
flashcards.answer: Most patients 94–98%. At risk of CO₂ retention (e.g. COPD): 88–92%.

critical.scenario: A 24-year-old asthmatic is tripoding, speaking 2–3 words, RR 32, HR 124, SpO₂ 89%, loud wheeze. After a nebulizer he becomes quiet: barely audible wheeze, RR 14, drowsy, SpO₂ 84%.
critical.question: What does this mean, and what now?

options.t: Respiratory failure: assist ventilation with a BVM and oxygen, call ALS, transport fast

options.f: Falling SpO₂ and drowsiness mean failure.

critical.explanation: A silent chest with falling consciousness is a pre-arrest sign.

critical.scenario: A 72-year-old has had a cough with green sputum for 4 days and fever today. HR 118, RR 28, SpO₂ 86%, BP 104/68, crackles at the right base, newly confused.
critical.question: What do you suspect, and the priority?

options.t: Pneumonia with possible sepsis: oxygen to target, sepsis screen, pre-alert and rapid transport

options.f: New confusion with infection is a red flag.
Fever and focal crackles point to pneumonia.

options.t: Give paracetamol and leave her home

critical.explanation: Fluids per protocol if hypotensive; watch for septic shock.

critical.scenario: A 45-year-old with a DVT two months ago stopped her blood thinners last week. Sudden sharp chest pain and breathlessness at rest, RR 32, SpO₂ 88%, HR 122. Swollen left calf.
critical.question: Most likely diagnosis and management?

options.t: Pulmonary embolism: oxygen to target, position of comfort, rapid transport, be ready for arrest

options.f: Never assume anxiety with this history.
Sudden onset with a DVT history is PE until proven otherwise.

options.t: Massage the calf to ease the pain

critical.explanation: Recent DVT and stopping anticoagulants are major risk factors.
